en: [1,1: The Monkey and the Wedge] There was a certain merchant who built a temple for a deity near a city.
There, the laborers, such as the master builders and others,
had entered the dining hall at midday for the purpose of eating.
By chance, a troop of monkeys arrived at the temple as an incidental visitor.

Now, there was a half-split wooden pillar made of *arjuna* wood belonging to a certain craftsman, which had been held steady by a wedge of *khadira* wood driven into its center with a mechanical device.
It remained there.
At one time, a troop of monkeys descended from a mountain peak and began to play at will among the treetops, the roofs of palaces, and heaps of wood.
But one among them, whose destruction was imminent, sat down out of fickleness and, pointing toward the movement of the mechanism on the pillar, said this:
"By whom has this peg been driven into the wrong place?"
Thus, grasping it with his very hands, he began to pull it out;
what occurred when the wedge moved from its place is not to be told.
"In this very way, it has been understood by you.
[1,2 The Jackal and the Drum]
There was a certain jackal whose throat was parched with hunger due to a lack of food; wandering here and there, he beheld the battlefield where both armies had fought,
and there he heard a great clamor.
With his heart agitated by that fear, he thought: "What is this?
I am ruined! Whose sound is this? Or where does it come from, and what kind of sound is it?"
While reflecting, he saw a drum shaped like a mountain peak;
and having seen it, he thought:
Is this sound inherent to it, or is it impelled by another?
Now, when she is touched by the tips of trees impelled by the wind—
"Then it makes a sound;
at other times it does not," he said, and remained silent.
But he drew near to her in order to discern whether she was substantial or insubstantial.
And out of curiosity, he himself struck both of their faces; and he thought:
"This is both accessible and edible for me."
Having thus resolved, he who was overcome by hunger tore [the skin] with one tusk;
yet, because of the toughness of the hide, he somehow did not suffer a breakage of his tusk. Having recovered, he thought once more:
"Surely there must be something edible inside her," he thought;
having thus resolved, he tore open the mouth of the drum and entered within,
but even there he found nothing at all.
Unable to turn back, with half his body submerged within, he laughed and said,
"I already knew this beforehand."

In a certain region, there was a wandering mendicant named Devaśarman; because he had accumulated many fine garments provided by numerous virtuous people, a great quantity of wealth came into his possession.
And he did not gain the confidence of anyone at all.
Then once, a man named Āṣāḍhabhūti, a thief of others' wealth, reflected, "How should I avoid this amount of property belonging to him? and approached him in the guise of a flatterer.
Having approached him at that time, he gained his confidence. Then, on one occasion, that wandering mendicant began to travel together with Āṣāḍhabhūti in the course of a pilgrimage.
There, in a certain part of the forest on the bank of a river, having stationed Āṣāḍhabhūti near his mother, he went off to a secluded spot to fetch water;
there he saw a great fight between two rams.
And seeing much blood fallen upon the ground from between the horns of those two, who were endowed with the power for incessant combat,
the jackal— his mind bound by hope and driven by greed for flesh— desired to seize it.
From the crushing and the subsequent striking, he immediately met his death.
Then the wandering mendicant, overcome with astonishment, said:
"The jackal [died] from the fighting of the *huḍu* goats."
Having performed his purification and arrived at that spot, Devaśarman did not see Āṣāḍhabhūti, who had already departed after grasping the mere essence of the meaning; he saw only—
He saw that his triple staff, water-pot, water-strainer, broom, and other implements had been cast aside, and he thought: "Where is this Āṣāḍhabhūti?"
"Surely I have been robbed by him," he said;
"and we [were robbed] by Āṣāḍhabhūti."
Then, as the sun was setting, he entered a certain village, reduced to nothing but fragments of skull-cups and knotted rags;
while entering, he saw a weaver living in solitude.
He requested a place to stay,
and he [the host] also pointed out a location for him in one part of his own house and [introduced] his wife.
She replied: "Until I have gone to the city, gathered with my friends, and finished drinking wine,
you must remain vigilant at home."
Having given these instructions, he departed.
Then his wife, a wanton woman incited by her female messenger, performed her bodily adornments and began to go into the presence of her paramour.
And her husband arrived, his speech interrupted by words faltering from intoxication, his gait unsteady, and his garments disarrayed.
Seeing him, Pratyutpannamati skillfully removed her ornaments.
Assuming his original form as before, he began the tasks of washing his feet, preparing his bed, and so forth;
meanwhile, the weaver entered his house and fell under the power of sleep.
Having woken from his sleep, he began to revile her:
"O harlot! My friends describe the misconduct directed toward you. Very well!"
Thinking, "I shall exercise restraint over this one who has grown fat," she too, being devoid of all bounds, began to give a reply;
and he, having awakened once more, [bound] her with a rope in the middle of her quiver.
Having made a firm connection, he fell asleep.
The female messenger urged him again to go;
she, however, having conceived an inspired thought, [acted] by means of an arrangement for her own appearance.
Having bound her, she went to the presence of the lover;
he too, having awakened, began to revile her in the same manner.
But the female messenger, with a suspicious heart and fearing the utterance of inappropriate words, said nothing.
She spoke thus;
but the weaver, thinking out of deceit, "This woman gives me no answer at all," rose up, cut off her nose with a sharp weapon, and said:
"Remain thus characterized;
who is asking after your welfare now?
Having said this, he fell under the power of sleep.
When the weaver woman arrived, she asked the female messenger:
"What is your news? What did he say when he woke up?"
"Speak! Speak! she said.
But the female messenger, having been punished, showed her nose and spoke with indignation:
"May all your news be auspicious."
"Release me;
I am going," she said.
When he had done so, she took her nose and departed.
The weaver also made himself appear as if bound by ropes;
however, the *kaulika* woke up exactly as before and reviled her. She too, being wicked, spoke back to him most insolently.
"Shame on you, wretch!
Who is capable of disfiguring me, who am innocent?
Let the World-Protectors hear me!"
"Just as I do not know any other man besides my husband from my youth, even in my mind,
by this truth may my face be free from blemish."
Thus it was said.
Then that fool, his mind deluded by those fabricated words, lit a torch and,
seeing his wife with her face uninjured, his eyes wide with joy, he kissed her.
With a joyful mind, he released him from his bonds, embraced him who had been oppressed, and helped him onto the bed;
meanwhile, the wandering mendicant had understood the matter exactly as it had occurred from the very beginning.
The female messenger, having had her nostrils cut off by hand, went to her own home and thought,
"What should be done now?
Then her husband, a barber, returned from the royal palace at dawn and said to his wife:
"Hand over the razor-case, my dear;
work must be done at the royal palace."
And that wicked woman, while remaining inside, sent forth a razor.
The barber, his mind possessed by anger because she had not handed over the entire set of razors, sent that very razor back at her in return.
Then, raising a loud cry of distress, wiping his nostrils with his hand,
and casting his nose— along with the falling blood— upon the ground, he said:
"Save me!"
"Save me!
I have been disfigured by this man through an unseen fault.
Thus, when the royal officers who had arrived saw her with their own eyes, they witnessed her condition.
The barber, who was deformed and had been severely beaten with stakes, heels, and clubs, was subsequently bound by the hands along with her and brought before the court of justice;
and when questioned by the officials, he said: "What is this great slaughter among one's own wife?"

When he did not provide an answer despite being told repeatedly, "This was done by you," the officials of justice commanded, "Let him be impaled on a stake. And seeing the blameless wandering mendicant, the barber, being led to the place of the stake, [the king thought:]
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he who had realized the true nature of reality approached the court and addressed those in charge of legal affairs:
"You ought not to impale this barber on a stake, for he has committed no fault."
For this reason,
let these three wonders be heard:
[the jackal by means of the ram-fight, and we by means of Āṣāḍhabhūti].
The female messenger and the weaver brought about three misfortunes for themselves;
however, the barber was rescued by those authorized officials who had realized the true nature of reality.
[1, 4: The Crow and the Snake]
In a certain place there was a tree,
and in it lived a pair of crows, husband and wife.

But at the time of their offspring's birth, a black snake would devour those young ones, which were still unable to move, as they crawled toward the opening of that tree-cavity. Then, out of resentment due to this injury, he [the mongoose] went to one dwelling at the foot of another tree.
He questioned his dear friend, the jackal, saying:
"My good sir, what do you consider to be the appropriate course of action now that things have come to this?
Because of the killing of our child, the two elders will surely perish, and with them, we ourselves shall cease to exist."
The jackal: [Having eaten many fish—superior, inferior, and middling—the crane, due to excessive greed, later died because of the grasp of a crab. (60)
The crow;
and how is this so? The jackal.
[1.5 The Heron and the Crab] There was a certain heron who, due to his old age, desiring a livelihood that required little effort, remained as if overcome by dejection at a certain part of a lake.
Standing there, displaying his own form,
a single crab surrounded by many fish said:
"My friends, why is the practice of taking food not being performed today as it was before?"
I am a crane; as one who eats fish,
I speak to you without that qualification.
Having encountered you previously, I protected my life;
today, however, my livelihood has been cut off,
and for this reason I am despondent.

Today, as fishermen were passing by this lake, they said:
"This pool contains many fish;
let us cast our nets into it."
"Other lakes near the city have not been found;
having found them, we will return," they said.
"Therefore, my good man, you are truly lost!"
"I too am utterly ruined by the loss of my livelihood.
Then he was addressed by them as follows:
"Wherever misfortune is heard of..."
From that very source, the means [to achieve it] is also obtained;
therefore, you ought to protect us.
Baka said:
"I am an egg-born creature and am incapable of opposing humans;
however, I shall lead you from this lake to another body of water.
Then, having gained confidence, O dear one, they followed him.
Brother! Uncle! Uncle! Lead me away!
"Take me! Take me first! he said.
That wicked-minded one, having led them there in succession, ate them one after another with great skill and attained the highest satisfaction.
But Kulīraka, agitated by the fear of death, entreated him again and again:
"O Master, you ought to rescue even me from the jaws of death.
But that evil-minded one thought:
"I am weary of this single-flavored fish-flesh;
I shall taste this particular delicacy as well.
Then, having lifted it up into the air and avoided all watery places, he set it down in one spot.
He descended onto the heated stone slab.
The crab, too, seeing the heap of remains from the fish's body he had previously eaten, thought to himself:
"Those fish have been deliberately killed by this evil-minded one.
Therefore, what is the appropriate course of action now?
Or rather—"
When a wise man, being attacked, sees no way out for himself while fighting, he should then die together with his enemy.
Even the crane, though ignorant of the crab’s grip with its pincers, through folly [fell victim].
He suffered the severing of his head at the hands of Kulīraka;
and Kulīraka, having seized the crane’s neck like a lotus stalk, set out toward the fish himself, his path marked by the feat of traveling through the air.
And they said to him,
"Brother, where is that man who calls himself my brother?
Then he replied:
He has met his death;
this is the head of that evil-souled one.
By means of that deception, he devoured many of your own kind.
"He too has perished because of me.
Therefore I say:
"Having devoured many fish..."
Then the crow said to the jackal,
"What do you consider to be the appropriate course of action for us two?
The jackal replied:
"Take this gold thread and place it here in the dwelling;
without doubt, its owner will have that black snake killed.
Having said this, the jackal departed.
Then the crow, searching for the golden thread, went toward Rājagṛha.
There, in a part of the inner apartments, he saw a costly golden thread set with excellent jewels, which had been washed by a maidservant and laid upon a pair of clean garments.
It was set down;
and having set it down, she began to converse with another woman.
But the crow, taking that [food], slowly showed himself through the air as he made his way toward his own abode.
He set out toward it.
Then, the tree was spotted by the guards, who were moving with great speed, spears, mallets, and lances in hand.
When he had placed it in his own nest,
one crow who was climbing up saw a black serpent [devouring] the young crows.
Having eaten it, he fell under the power of sleep;
while he was thus asleep, he was killed by him.
Having done that, [the thief] took the golden thread and departed.
[1.6 The Lion and the Hare] There was once a great lion living in a certain forest. He constantly caused the destruction of the deer.
Then all those deer, facing him with humble hearts, holding blades of green grass in their mouths, and resting their knees upon the ground, made this request to the king of deer:
"O King of Beasts, what is the use of this cruel act of yours toward your master, which is contrary to the next world and consists of the causeless slaughter of all deer?
We ourselves are already as good as lost."
For you too there will be a lack of food;
thus, there will be affliction for both of us.
Therefore, be appeased.
"We, however, O Master, shall send one forest-dweller at a time from our own species by turn.
When this was done, in the course of time, the turn of the hare arrived.
Commanded by all the deer, he, with a mind full of resentment, reflected:
"This is my end; it is an entry into the jaws of death. What course of action is now appropriate for me?"
"Or rather, what is impossible for the wise?
I myself shall kill the lion by some stratagem. Having thought this, he waited until the time for the lion's meal had passed and then departed.

He too, his throat parched with hunger, his eyes bloodshot with rage, his face terrifying with bared fangs from the gnashing of his teeth and trembling, and causing fear by the manner of his lashing tail, spoke to him.
What can even those who are utterly enraged do other than deprive one of life? You are already as good as dead today;
what is this delay of yours?
The hare said:
"My lord, the time for my meal has passed; it was not transgressed while I was under my own control."
A lion: "By whom have you been restrained? A hare: [He replied:
"By a lion."
Regarding the phrase "by a lion":
having heard that, the lion, his heart filled with extreme agitation, said,
"How can there be another lion here in this forest protected by my own arms?"
The hare said, "Very well.
Then the lion thought,
"What purpose is served by killing this one for me?"
"I shall show him that rival;
and having slain him, I will eat him.
Thus he spoke to him.
"Show that wicked-souled one to me.

Then that hare, laughing inwardly and taking the treatises on statecraft (*nītiśāstra*) of Bṛhaspati and Uśanas as his authority, for the sake of achieving his own purpose, [approached] a place endowed with pure water.
He showed him a large well, built of bricks, with water reaching a depth of two men's height; and he, because he did not recognize the reflection of his own body,
with a mind set upon a wrong path, thinking "this is that rival," suddenly [attacked] him.
Having climbed upon it, he met his death through folly.
There was once a certain king who possessed a bed endowed with every excellence, the like of which existed nowhere else.
On a portion of that bed-covering lived a louse named Mandavisarpiṇī. Then, a bug named Tiṇṭibha, driven by the wind, alighted there;
he [found] that bed to have an exceedingly fine upper cover and two pillows.
Seeing the vast, exceedingly soft, and fragrant sands of the Jāhnavī, he attained supreme satisfaction;
his mind drawn by the touch of that sand, he wandered here and there until, with great difficulty, he was [reunited] with her.
He was accompanied by Mandavisarpiṇī,
who said to him:
"From where have you come to this unsuitable dwelling?"
"Depart from here!
"O bedbug!
Noble lady, I have already tasted many kinds of flesh here."
And there are the bloods residing within the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras;
they are indeed coarse, slimy, disagreeable, and unpleasant.
Furthermore, there is the presiding deity of this bed.
His blood will become delightful and like nectar,
through the constant efforts of physicians and the application of medicines and other treatments.

Through the suppression of wind, bile, and phlegm, he attained freedom from disease by means of foods that were unctuous, delicate, and liquid, seasoned with sugar, jaggery, pomegranate, the three pungents,
and salt, and enriched with the potent flesh of terrestrial, aquatic, and aerial animals.
"I consider this accumulated blood to be like an elixir;
since it is fragrant and nourishing, I wish to taste it through your favor."
Therefore, she, speaking with slow and hesitant words, said:
"This is impossible for those like you, who have fire in your mouths and subsist on biting;
depart from this bed."
Then he fell at her feet; out of courtesy, she agreed, saying, "So be it," but added,
"However, you must not strike him at an improper time, nor on his most tender parts."
He said:
"What is its time?
I am ignorant of it because I am unacquainted with it."
She, however, said:
"When you have fallen asleep from the fatigue of drinking wine and are lying fast asleep from the intensity of amorous play, you must examine [the matter] very gently and softly."
"His body overcome by intoxication, fatigue, and sleep, he did not wake quickly. When this was established, he was bitten at that very first watch of the night by one who knew no time;
that king, too, had the region of his belly shriveled up as if burnt by a firebrand.
Rising up in great agitation, he said, "Alas! I have been bitten by someone!
Then the bug, startled by the king's words, descended from the bed.
Having taken refuge in another opening,

she was discovered and killed by the bed-chamber attendants, who, acting on their master’s command, were searching most thoroughly while changing the bedding; thus, the slow-moving woman, hidden within, was found and slain.
[1.8 The Blue Jackal] In the vicinity of a certain city, there lived a jackal named Caṇḍarava who used to sleep inside a nearby hole.
Once, while searching for food, he reached the city at night; with his throat parched by hunger and his eyes closed, he wandered and entered the city.
And by the dogs dwelling in that city—
With his limbs being torn apart by the tips of sharp fangs,
filling the hollows of the directions with terrifying howls of fear, he stumbled and fled hither and thither until, out of ignorance, he fell into a jar of indigo dye.
The pack of dogs departed as they had come,
and he too, with great difficulty due to the remainder of his life, rose up from that vat of indigo.
Then, seeing his body dyed with the juice of indigo, those standing nearby—
The packs of jackals, their eyes trembling with fear, fled in all directions, wondering, "Who is this?
He, too, thought to himself:
"Surely these people are fleeing upon seeing this transformation of my form. Then, with a steady mind, he spoke to them softly: "Enough of this agitation!"
"By the command of Indra, I have come to the surface of the earth, capable of protecting the entire multitude of beasts of prey.
Then, having heard those words—
The hosts of beasts of prey— lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, hares, deer, wildcats, jackals, and so forth— bowed down to him;
and every day, with the flesh of intoxicated elephants torn apart by the thunderbolt-like claws of the maned lion, [they offered him sustenance].

With his belly filled, he cast that pack of jackals outside like a mere thicket and brought the lions, tigers, and others who were nearby within his reach. Once, however, having satisfied his hunger with various kinds of flesh, [he looked] toward those situated in all directions.

Hearing the cry of the howling jackals, he roared even more loudly and swiftly; thereupon those lions and others, overcome with shame, cast their eyes toward the ground and thought, "Alas, what a pity!
We have been deceived."
Having determined that "this is a jackal," they destroyed him with harsh words out of anger. [1,9 Camel, Lion]
[The Story of the Panther,
the Crow, and the Jackal]:
Once, in a certain part of a forest, there lived a lion named Madotkaṭa.
He had three flesh-eating followers—a leopard, a crow, and a jackal.
While they were wandering about, they saw a camel that had strayed from its caravan;
and seeing it, whose appearance was unfamiliar to them and which provoked laughter, the lion—
He asked:
"Let this unprecedented being here in the forest be questioned:
'Who are you?'"
Then the crow, having understood the true state of affairs, said,
"This is a camel whose name has been told. Thereupon, he was brought into the presence of the lion after being inspired with confidence.
He, in turn, related exactly what had happened regarding his separation from the caravan leader;
and the lion granted him his favor and bestowed upon him a promise of safety.
While things were proceeding in this manner, once upon a time, the lion—
His body wounded by the tusks in a fight with a wild elephant, he became a cave-dweller;
and when five or six days had passed, they all fell into a state of extreme distress due to the lack of food.
Since they were thus dejected,
the lion said to them:
"Because of this ailment, I am no longer able to provide food for you as I did before."
"Therefore, you yourselves should at least rise up for your own sake.
They said to him,
"Since things are thus, what is the use of nourishing ourselves?"
"O lion!
Excellent is your conduct as a subordinate, and great is your devotion toward me. What you have said is most admirable."
"You are capable,
while I am afflicted with illness;
therefore, please bring food for me in this condition."
And when they said nothing at all, he addressed them:
"What is the use of this embarrassment?"
"Let some creature be sought out;
even in this state, I shall provide for you and for myself the means of sustenance."
Having spoken thus, they too rose up and entered another part of the forest together with Krathanaka.
Setting Krathanaka aside, they began to plot an evil counsel.
Thereupon, the crow said:
"We have been ruined by this master, even though the matter was within our own control. They both asked,
"How so?"
He said, "Is this not Krathanaka?
They replied: [Yes].
"This one has come to us for refuge with full confidence and has been granted the status of a friend.
He replied,
"Those who feed on grass and those who feed on flesh have an incompatible relationship."
Then the two of them said:
"He is protected by our master through the granting of safety;
therefore, this is both improper and impossible."
The crow spoke again:
"Stay here while I myself shall accomplish this matter.
Having said this, he went into the presence of the lion.
And the lion said,
"Have you searched for any living being? The crow replied:
Whoever possesses eyes or strength, let him search;
but we are all indeed blind due to the lack of food, and our strength is utterly exhausted.
However, I must certainly inform you that the time has come:
my master has destroyed himself by his own hand regarding a matter that was within his own power—
just like a lion.
"How so?
"A crow. "But surely this is a *krathanaka*!"
A lion!
This is a tragedy; this is a cruel act!
I have granted him protection and fearlessness;
moreover:
"Neither the gift of cows nor the gift of land..."
Indeed, the gift of food is not as preeminent as they say here that the gift of fearlessness is the most preeminent among all gifts. (117)
The crow said: "Oh, how brilliant is my master’s insight regarding the treatises on Dharma!
This is yet another preeminent statement of the Great Sages."
Just as an inferior undertaking may be for the sake of something superior;
and it has also been said:
"One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of one's own self.
Furthermore, he said:
"Let not my master kill him himself;
I have begun his slaughter by means of a stratagem.
[Thus spoke] the lion.
How so? Like a crow; for this crow, having seen its master in such a state as well as us, [behave] itself...
He offered himself for the sake of nourishing others, for his own journey to heaven, and for the welfare of sentient beings.
When the crow had spoken thus, the lion, as if struck by a confusion of mind, did not utter a single word in reply.
He, in turn, went back to them and informed each one with fabricated words,
saying: "When you have gone into the presence of the lion, you must speak thus."
Then, having made a pact with Krathanaka, they went into the presence of the lion.

A lion named Vajradanta used to dwell there.

"Therefore, I request something from you,
